::: {.lesson-meta}
Part 2 · Lesson 2 · About 50 minutes
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Analogy: a postal system for flats"}
An **IP address** is a building's street address. A **port** is the flat number inside the building: one computer runs many programs, each listening at its own flat number. **TCP** is a registered-mail service that numbers every page, confirms delivery, and re-sends lost pages, so the letter arrives complete and in order. **DNS** is the phone book that turns a name you can remember (`github.com`) into the street address the post office actually needs.
:::

## IP addresses

Every device on a network has an **IP address**. The common format, IPv4, is four numbers from 0 to 255: `140.82.114.3`. The newer IPv6 format is longer (`2606:50c0:8000::153`) because the world ran out of IPv4 addresses.

Some addresses are special:

| Address | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `127.0.0.1` (name: `localhost`) | "this same computer". Traffic never leaves the machine. |
| `10.x.x.x`, `172.16-31.x.x`, `192.168.x.x` | **private** addresses, used inside home and company networks and cloud VPCs (Part 7). Not reachable from the internet directly. |
| `0.0.0.0` | when a server listens on it: "accept connections on every network interface" |

A server bound to `127.0.0.1` is reachable only from the same machine; bound to `0.0.0.0`, it's reachable from outside too. That one detail causes many "my server works locally but nobody else can reach it" problems, including inside Docker containers (lesson 7.1).

## Ports

One machine runs many network programs at once, so each one listens on a **port**, a number from 1 to 65535. Well-known services have conventional ports:

| Port | Service |
|---|---|
| 22 | SSH (lesson 2.4) |
| 80 | HTTP |
| 443 | HTTPS |
| 5432 | PostgreSQL (Part 3) |
| 6379 | Redis (Part 5) |
| 8000 | FastAPI during development (Part 4) |

A connection is identified by both ends: (your IP, your port) to (server IP, server port). Your side's port is picked automatically from a high range. Only one program can listen on a given port at a time:

```text
OSError: [Errno 98] Address already in use
```

When you see that, another process (often an old copy of your own server) already holds the port.

## TCP: reliable conversations

Data travels across networks in small **packets**. Packets can be lost, duplicated or arrive out of order. **TCP** (Transmission Control Protocol) builds a reliable two-way stream on top: it numbers the bytes, acknowledges what arrived, re-sends what didn't, and reassembles everything in order.

Before any data flows, the two sides agree to talk with a **handshake**:

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant S as Server (listening on a port)
  C->>S: SYN ("can we talk?")
  S-->>C: SYN-ACK ("yes, can you hear me?")
  C->>S: ACK ("yes")
  Note over C,S: connection open: both can send bytes
  C->>S: data
  S-->>C: data
  C->>S: FIN ("I'm done")
```

That handshake costs a round trip before the first byte of data. It's one reason reusing connections (as `httpx.Client` does) makes repeated requests faster.

**UDP** is the alternative: no handshake, no guarantees, just fire packets. It suits live video and games, where a late packet is useless anyway. Almost everything in this course uses TCP.

## A client and a server, in 20 lines

Python's `socket` module talks TCP directly. The server:

```python
# echo_server.py
import socket

with socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM) as server:
    server.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
    server.bind(("127.0.0.1", 9000))
    server.listen()
    print("listening on 127.0.0.1:9000", flush=True)
    connection, address = server.accept()
    with connection:
        print(f"connection from {address}", flush=True)
        data = connection.recv(1024)
        connection.sendall(b"echo: " + data)
```

The client:

```python
# echo_client.py
import socket

with socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", 9000)) as connection:
    connection.sendall(b"hello server")
    print(connection.recv(1024).decode("utf-8"))
```

Run the server in one terminal and the client in another:

```text
$ python3 echo_server.py
listening on 127.0.0.1:9000
connection from ('127.0.0.1', 49696)
```
```text
$ python3 echo_client.py
echo: hello server
```

- `AF_INET` means IPv4; `SOCK_STREAM` means TCP.
- `bind` claims the address and port; `listen` starts accepting; `accept` waits for one client and returns a new connection for it.
- `49696` is the client's automatically chosen port.
- Sockets send **bytes** (`b"..."`), not strings: you encode and decode explicitly (lesson 1.7).
- `SO_REUSEADDR` lets you restart the server immediately instead of waiting for the OS to release the port.

Every web server, database and message queue in this course is, underneath, this pattern: a process listening on a port, accepting TCP connections, reading bytes and writing bytes back. What differs is the **protocol**: the agreed format of those bytes. HTTP (next lesson) is one.

## DNS: names to addresses

You type `github.com`, but TCP needs an IP address. **DNS** (Domain Name System) translates. Your computer asks a DNS **resolver** (usually run by your internet provider or network), which looks the name up in a worldwide hierarchy of servers and caches the answer for a while.

```text
$ getent hosts github.com
140.82.114.3    github.com
```

```python
import socket

print(socket.gethostbyname("api.github.com"))
```
```text
140.82.114.6
```

(Big services have many addresses; you may get a different one.) `dig github.com` or `nslookup github.com` show more detail if they're installed.

When "the site is down" for you but not for others, DNS is a frequent suspect. In Part 7, you'll point your own domain name at your AWS deployment with DNS records.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A["httpx.get('https://api.github.com/...')"] --> D[DNS: api.github.com?]
  D -->|140.82.114.6| T[TCP connect to 140.82.114.6:443]
  T --> L[TLS handshake: encrypt the connection]
  L --> H[HTTP request and response]
```

That chain (DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP) is what happens on every web request. The next lesson covers the last two.

## Common mistakes

- **Server bound to `127.0.0.1` when you need outside access** (or the reverse: exposed to the world when it should be local only).
- **"Address already in use"**: an old process still holds the port. Find it with `lsof -i :9000` or `ss -ltnp`, and stop it.
- **Treating bytes as strings** with sockets. Encode before sending, decode after receiving.
- **Assuming `recv(1024)` returns a whole message.** TCP is a stream: a message can arrive in several pieces. Real protocols mark where messages end (HTTP uses `Content-Length`, for example).

## Check yourself

**1.** Why can two different programs on one machine both be network servers?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
They listen on different ports. The IP address identifies the machine; the port identifies the program on it.
:::

**2.** What does TCP add on top of raw packets?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A reliable, ordered, two-way byte stream: it numbers the data, acknowledges receipt, re-sends lost packets, and reassembles them in order. It also opens connections with a handshake and closes them cleanly.
:::

**3.** Your FastAPI server runs inside a container, listening on `127.0.0.1:8000`, and nothing outside the container can reach it. Why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`127.0.0.1` inside the container means "this container only". The server must listen on `0.0.0.0` to accept connections from outside it. You'll set exactly this in lesson 7.1.
:::

## Exercise

Change the echo server so it handles **several clients one after another** (loop around `accept`), replying in upper case, and stops when a client sends `quit`. Test it with three client runs.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```python
import socket

with socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM) as server:
    server.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
    server.bind(("127.0.0.1", 9000))
    server.listen()
    while True:
        connection, address = server.accept()
        with connection:
            message = connection.recv(1024).decode("utf-8")
            if message == "quit":
                connection.sendall(b"bye")
                break
            connection.sendall(message.upper().encode("utf-8"))
```

This server handles one client at a time: a slow client blocks everyone else. Lesson 2.6 is about doing many things at once.
:::

## Stretch

Use `socket.getaddrinfo("github.com", 443)` to list every address returned for GitHub on port 443. How many are there, and which are IPv4 versus IPv6?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
```python
import socket

for family, _, _, _, address in socket.getaddrinfo("github.com", 443, proto=socket.IPPROTO_TCP):
    print(family.name, address)
```

`AF_INET` entries are IPv4, `AF_INET6` are IPv6. The count depends on your network and DNS resolver; some networks return only IPv4.
:::
